selected_news.source_headline: India Calls Out Turkiye Over Exclusion From UNGA Draft Consultations On UN-OIC Cooperation
selected_news.article_text: India Calls Out Turkiye Over Exclusion From UNGA Draft Consultations On UN-OIC Cooperation United Nations, Nov 17: India has raised strong objections over Turkiye's "blatant and intentional" decision to exclude New Delhi and other member states from consultations on a resolution on cooperation between the UN and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC)... United Nations, Nov 17: India has raised strong objections over Turkiye's "blatant and intentional" decision to exclude New Delhi and other member states from consultations on a resolution on cooperation between the UN and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and voted against the draft in the General Assembly. The draft resolution 'Cooperation between the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation', introduced by Iraq, was adopted Monday by a recorded vote, with 112 nations voting in favour, six against, and 39 countries abstaining. India, along with Armenia, Cyprus, Greece, Israel and the United States, voted against the resolution. Turkiye was the resolution's facilitator. Apart from India, other countries, including Cyprus and Greece, also called out Ankara's "lack of transparency and inclusivity" throughout the draft's negotiation process. India's Deputy Permanent Representative at the UN Ambassador Yojna Patel said the Permanent Observer Mission of the OIC chose to exclude the Indian delegation and a number of other countries when circulating successive drafts of the resolution. Delivering the explanation of vote, Patel strongly called out the working methods adopted by the resolution's facilitator, describing it as a "concerning matter" and calling for an investigation into the process. "My delegation has voted against this resolution not only because of its substantive aspects, but also for an even more concerning matter regarding the working methods adopted by the facilitator who convened negotiations on the same," Patel said. Strongly criticising the lack of inclusive intergovernmental negotiations over the resolution, she expressed her "deep dismay" that the "Permanent Observer Mission" of the OIC "chose to exclude not only my delegation but a number of other countries when circulating successive drafts of the resolution. "This is not only shocking but also sets a bad precedent of delegations excluding specific member states to enable their agendas." Patel further said that despite some delegations registering their objections in subsequent rounds, the "facilitators still chose to not include select countries." Other basic procedures such as acknowledging inputs were also "blatantly disregarded, indicating that it was done by design rather than by mistake. She said it was "unfortunate that there are member states who publicly profess commitment to multilateralism and completely turn a blind eye to its core guiding principles." Underlining that the UN was founded on the principles of sovereign equality, inclusivity and multilateral cooperation, Patel said differences of position among member states are inherent to multilateral diplomacy and "cannot, in themselves, justify blatant and intentional exclusion from the consultations on matters before the General Assembly." "My delegation strongly objects to such working methods that try to hoodwink excluded delegations into believing that this was just a technical update, which it was not," she said. India has called on the UN General Assembly President "to investigate this and prevent its recurrence." Questioning the substance of the resolution, New Delhi further said the draft claimed to foster solutions to other conflicts. "The rationale for seeking to extend the role of OIC in this manner is unclear. The OIC is not a regional organisation," Patel said. India expressed concern over a reference in the resolution about the ninth session of the OIC Ministerial Conference on Women held in July this year in Islamabad. During that conference, a declaration was adopted that made references to Jammu and Kashmir. Patel said that India "rejects" the declaration and the omnibus resolution adopted at the conference. "The resolution contains reference to documents and statements that have unwarranted and factually incorrect references to my country. Such documents, unfortunately, reflect the continued misuse of the OIC platform for narrow political ends. The OIC has no locus standi to comment on India's internal affairs," Patel said. In a thinly veiled reference to Pakistan, India voiced regret that the OIC has "once again allowed itself to be systematically misused by one Member State to weaponise OIC resolutions and declarations against India through false and baseless allegations. Pakistan is a founding and prominent member of the 57-member OIC. "India calls upon the OIC to uphold the principles of objectivity, constructive dialogue, and mutual respect, and to ensure that its outcomes do not become a vehicle for the pursuit of narrow political agendas," Patel said. India "believes that sovereign member states take care of the interests of their citizens regardless of their faith. We do not recognise that only co-religionists can protect the interests of adherents of their faith. Such regressive views have no place in today's world, and especially at this forum," Patel said. In its explanation of vote, Cyprus voiced deep regret over the "lack of transparency and inclusivity by Turkiye as the facilitator of this resolution throughout the negotiation process." "We strongly regret that Cyprus has been repeatedly excluded from the communication on this process and subsequently from the negotiation process of this resolution. Despite our best efforts and requests, inclusion of all UN Member States in this negotiation process is not a matter of political discretion of the facilitator, but a principle enshrined in the UN Charter," the Cyprus delegate said. Greece also raised "serious concerns" regarding the conduct of negotiations under Turkiye's facilitation. "Throughout the process, the European Union submitted comments and amendments in good faith, which were neither meaningfully addressed nor accompanied by substantial explanations for their rejection. Furthermore, revised drafts were circulated without adequate consultation," Greece's delegate said. Greece also objected to its exclusion, along with certain delegations, from the circulation of draft texts. "Such practices fall short of the transparency, inclusivity and good faith expected in General Assembly negotiations. We strongly believe they are not representative of our member states." The US hoped that future versions of the OIC resolution "will eliminate excessive and redundant language and contentious issues and instead focus on direct and concrete areas of cooperation that can achieve consensus." Ireland, delivering the explanation of vote on behalf of the European Union, said the bloc and its member states regret the "lack of transparency and inclusivity throughout the negotiation process, despite requests to be included in the consultations. "The EU and several of its member states were excluded from relevant communications and were consequently not afforded a meaningful opportunity to participate in the negotiations," it said. (Agencies)

selected_news.title: NASA CRS-25: Cygnus XL 29 Kasım’da Fırlatılıyor
selected_news.summary: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission launched Saturday, April 11, 2026, aboard the company’s Cygnus XL spacecraft atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. Credit: Northrop Grumman NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23. Filled with approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, the Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25. After arriving at the International Space Station, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, who are living and working aboard the space station, will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture the Cygnus XL on Tuesday, Dec. 1. Ground controllers then will install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. NASA’s live launch and docking coverage will stream through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Highlights of space station research and technology demonstrations being delivered aboard this Cygnus XL spacecraft include experiments to improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, predict cancer spread, and advance treatments for muscle loss, as well as improve radiation sensing and advance food production for future long-duration missions. The spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the orbiting laboratory until May 2027, then depart with several thousand pounds of disposal items and other unneeded cargo, burning up harmlessly during re-entry. Northrop Grumman named the spacecraft the S.S. James “Jim” A. Lovell in honor of the former NASA astronaut. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon. Monday, Nov. 23 12 p.m.: Prelaunch teleconference will stream on NASA’s YouTube channel with the following participants: Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program Jennifer Buchli, chief scientist, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program Dave Schiller, vice president, civil space and sciences, Northrop Grumman Jared Metter, director, flight reliability, SpaceX To participate in the teleconference, media must contact the NASA Johnson Space Center newsroom for call details by 11 a.m., Nov. 23, at: jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov or 281-483-5111. To ask questions, media must dial in no later than 10 minutes before the start of the call. The agency’s media credentialing policy is available online. Additional prelaunch updates will be available on NASA’s space station blog . Sunday, Nov. 29 10:25 a.m.: Launch coverage begins 10:47 a.m.: Launch Tuesday, Dec. 1 1:10 a.m.: Arrival coverage begins 2:35 a.m.: Capture NASA website launch coverage Launch day coverage of the mission will be available on the NASA website . Coverage will include live streaming and blog updates beginning no earlier than 10 a.m. on Nov. 29, as the countdown milestones occur. On-demand streaming video on NASA+ and photos of the launch will be available shortly after liftoff. For questions about countdown coverage, contact the NASA Kennedy Space Center newsroom at 321-867-2468. Follow countdown coverage on our International Space Station blog for updates. Attend launch virtually Members of the public can register to attend this launch virtually. NASA’s virtual guest program for this mission also includes curated launch resources, notifications about related opportunities or changes, and a stamp for the NASA virtual guest passport following launch. Watch, engage on social media Let people know you’re watching the mission on X, Facebook, and Instagram by following and tagging these accounts: X: @ NASA, @ NASAKennedy , @NASASpaceOps , @ Space_Station , @ ISS National Lab Facebook: NASA , NASAKennedy , ISS , ISS National Lab Instagram: @ NASA , @ NASAKennedy , @ ISS , @ ISSNationalLab Learn more about this commercial resupply services mission at: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/nasas-northrop-grumman-crs-25/ -end- Josh Finch / Jimi Russell Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1100 joshua.a.finch@nasa.gov / james.j.russell@nasa.gov Steven Siceloff Kennedy Space Center, Fla. 321-876-2468 steven.p.siceloff@nasa.gov Sandra Jones Johnson Space Center, Houston 281-483-5111 sandra.p.jones@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 18, 2026 Editor Jessica Taveau Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Commercial Resupply International Space Station (ISS) ISS Research Johnson Space Center Kennedy Space Center

selected_news.title: Anthropic, hisse satışıyla 19,3 bn dolar kazanacak
selected_news.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
selected_news.source_headline: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
selected_news.article_text: In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy? In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious" Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity" Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston
